item.title: Tropical Cyclone Wind Field Diagnosis with Image-to-Image Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.00038v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This study presents a novel application of image-to-image generative adversarial networks (GANs) to produce a complete tropical cyclone (TC) surface wind field diagnosis from a single frame of satellite infrared brightness temperature (IR). Because TC surface wind fields are infrequently observed, we train on two data sets. The first contains 3,323 image pairs of IR and wind fields from Weather Research and Forecasting Model (WRF) simulations (WRF2WRF). The second contains 11,886 real IR satellite images paired with parametric wind fields built on the extended best-track data set (IBTrACS) of TC intensities and wind radii (GOES2PARA). Both models, conditioned on storm intensity, motion, and latitude, transform single-channel IR into wind fields over 6$^{\circ} \times$ 6$^{\circ}$ (WRF2WRF) and 7$^{\circ} \times$ 7$^{\circ}$ (GOES2PARA) domains, at 256 $\times$ 256 pixel resolution. GOES2PARA captures outer wind field asymmetries, enabling diagnosis of 64, 50, and 34-knot wind radii (R64, R50, R34) in each quadrant. WRF2WRF also produces detailed rainbands and eyewall asymmetries. Pixel-wise RMSE against held out truth demonstrates realistic wind field generation with mean RMSE of 6.4 knots (GOES2PARA) and 7.2 knots (WRF2WRF). Compared against IBTrACS, WRF2WRF achieved mean absolute errors (MAE) of 14.8 nautical miles (NM) for radius of maximum wind (RMW) and 25.9 NM for R34. GOES2PARA achieved 10.0 NM MAE for RMW and 25.9 NM for R34. Against Synthetic Aperture Radar wind fields GOES2PARA yielded a lower mean pixel-wise error (RMSE 12.1 kt, MAE 9.5 kt) than WRF2WRF (RMSE 13.9 kt, MAE 11.3 kt). Unlike many existing operational surface wind speed algorithms, our image-to-image models provide updated wind fields with every new satellite image.
item.dc:creator: Sarah J. Ollier, David S. Nolan, Brian D. McNoldy, Eduardo Siman

item.title: The role of salinity in Snowball Earth: A simplified coupled atmosphere--ocean--ice model
item.description: arXiv:2611.00357v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Neoproterozoic Snowball Earth events represent among the most extreme climate states in Earth's history, with ice covering all or nearly all of the ocean. Despite its control on the seawater freezing point and on the partitioning of water between the ocean and ice, salinity has not been well-represented in Snowball Earth models---typically prescribed, simplified, or ignored. Sea-glacier dynamics under open-ocean conditions have similarly lacked adequate treatment. We extend the one-dimensional coupled atmosphere-ocean-ice model of Pollard and Kasting (2005, J. Geophys. Res. Oceans 110, C07010) by adding prognostic latitudinal salinity dynamics, global ocean mass conservation and salt conservation, and a revised sea-glacier momentum equation, along with a greenhouse-gas term allowing transitions between full-snowball and partially open-ocean states. The model produces two equilibrium states exhibiting strong hysteresis under varying greenhouse forcing. Higher initial ocean salinity systematically lowers the CO$_2$ thresholds for both the onset and the termination of glaciation, reflecting freezing-point depression and coupled dynamics among salinity, ocean volume, and marine ice thickness. Under full glaciation, the shrinking ocean becomes hypersaline, feeding back on thermal structure and equilibrium ice thickness. Across a 72-case factorial ensemble spanning Neoproterozoic-relevant ranges, a marginal-effect analysis shows that only ice albedo shifts the thresholds more than initial salinity (69.1\% and 80.5\% versus 21.3\% and 9.7\% for initiation and deglaciation), followed by the solar constant (8.9\% and 5.6\%) and geothermal heat flux (0.6\% and 4.2\%). Salinity should therefore be treated as an active variable in studies of Snowball thresholds.
item.dc:creator: Sounav Sengupta, Francisco E. Spaulding-Astudillo, Dorian S. Abbot, Eli Tziperman, Yosef Ashkenazy

item.title: An all-weather microwave-based AI retrieval of pan-Arctic melt pond fraction
item.description: arXiv:2611.00940v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Melt pond fraction (MPF) is a key variable governing Arctic sea ice albedo and seasonal sea ice predictability, yet existing pan-Arctic MPF products rely almost exclusively on optical sensors, limiting availability under cloud cover and seasonal darkness. This study presents PRISM-MPF, the first pan-Arctic, multi-year, all-weather MPF dataset, derived from PRISM (Polar Retrievals through Intelligent Sensor Merging), a machine learning framework fusing multi-source microwave observations with auxiliary thermal and spatiotemporal information to complement optical products. An XGBoost model was trained on eight melt seasons (2017-2025, excluding 2019) using Sentinel-1 C-band SAR backscatter, AMSR2 brightness temperatures and sea ice concentration, NOAA OISST sea surface temperature, and spatiotemporal descriptors (date and grid position). Three experiments assessed baseline skill and feature importance, independent sensor-group contributions (including CryoSat-2 radar freeboard), and regional specialisation, all under Leave-One-Year-Out (LOYO) cross-validation on unseen melt seasons. The baseline retrieval achieved a per-season mean R2=0.468 and RMSE=0.080 (pooled over 1,066,808 pixels: R2=0.532, RMSE=0.077), comparable to prior regional microwave-based studies, now at pan-Arctic, multi-year scale. Removing spatiotemporal features or C-band SAR reduced skill comparably (Delta R2=+0.089 and +0.085), whereas physical sensors alone outperformed spatiotemporal features alone (R2=0.375 vs 0.261), showing the two groups are complementary. Regional specialisation offered no advantage over a single pan-Arctic retrieval. This framework establishes a reproducible foundation for all-weather Arctic MPF monitoring, extensible to new sensors, longer records, and reference products.
item.dc:creator: Sara Apar\'icio, Simon Driscoll, Mark R. Drinkwater, Daniela Flocco

item.title: Jovian Polar Vortex Generation in a Shallow-Water Model with Quasi-Stochastic Convection
item.description: arXiv:2611.02372v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The mechanisms governing the formation and maintenance of polar vortices on Saturn and Jupiter represent a significant challenge in current planetary atmospheric dynamics. In the presence of internal heat sources, the existence of condensable components leads to widespread moist convection in the polar regions of these gas giants. However, the role of moist convective organization in the formation and maintenance of such polar vortices remains poorly understood. To investigate the interaction between convection and polar vortices, this study develops a polar $\gamma$-plane shallow-water model coupled with a quasi-stochastic convective parameterization. In this quasi-stochastic scheme, convection is prescribed as localized impulsive mass sinks, with the inception probability depending on local vorticity, thereby assigning a higher convective likelihood to cyclonic regions. Numerical experiments successfully reproduce shielded cyclones and persistent vortex crystals reminiscent of Jupiter's polar configuration. Increasing mesoscale feedback promotes vortex growth, shield formation, and spectral organization, while the characteristic vortex scale depends on both the deformation radius and the convective parameterization. The resulting patterns exhibit both clockwise and counterclockwise structural drift, whose direction and rate are not adequately captured by a conventional Rossby wave phase-speed estimate. A Biot--Savart diagnostic reveals competing contributions to structural drift, with predominantly counterclockwise advection induced by the other vortices and clockwise advection induced by the background vorticity outside the identified vortices. These results provide a possible formation pathway for shielded vortex crystals and highlight the role of convective feedback in vortex formation.
item.dc:creator: Ruan Yuhang, Fu Hao, Li Cheng, Yang Da

item.title: New Wine in an Old Bottle -- NeuralPOM: A Hybrid Ocean Forecast Model with Differentiable Dynamics and Staged Learning
item.description: arXiv:2611.02460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coarse-grid ocean circulation models rely on empirical subgrid parameterizations that struggle to capture mesoscale eddies, whereas purely data-driven neural forecasters accumulate trajectory drift, violate tracer conservation, and damp small-scale variability over extended integrations. Here we present NeuralPOM, a hybrid ocean forecast model that couples differentiable explicit mode-split and semi-implicit free-surface implementations of the Princeton Ocean Model (POM) to a conservation-constrained neural corrector. The three-dimensional primitive-equation solver advances the ocean state, while the neural network periodically updates the physical fields at high-frequency (1 h) or low-frequency (1 day) intervals under volume, heat, and salt conservation constraints. Using a fine-grid reference dataset exceeding 100,000 model days in a wind-driven double-gyre basin, we introduce a three-stage training procedure comprising offline single-step pretraining, multi-step differentiable training through the ocean solver, and multi-day closed-loop rollout training. Over 100-day forecasts, NeuralPOM reduces errors across all prognostic fields relative to coarse-grid physical closures and direct neural forecasters, preserving mesoscale kinetic energy while improving eddy phase alignment. Controlled ablations show that closed-loop training suppresses multi-day drift, whereas backpropagating gradients through the differentiable solver stabilizes high-frequency coupling. Finally, because high-frequency tracer updates can introduce density anomalies via the equation of state that excite spurious baroclinic pressure gradients, we introduce Density-Normal Damping (DND) to attenuate the density-modifying (diapycnal) tracer component while retaining the density-compensated (isopycnal) correction.
item.dc:creator: Ruiqi Shu, Guangliang Liu, Ruijian Gou, Tianrun Gao, Haomin Wen, Hao Li, Xiaomeng Huang

item.title: Six-hourly Probabilistic Precipitation Forecasts Created From Hourly Probabilities
item.description: arXiv:2611.03326v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A lightweight neural network is described that produces six-hourly, spatially detailed probabilistic quantitative precipitation forecasts (PQPF) from a sequence of hourly spatially detailed probabilistic forecasts, for lead times from 6 to 72\,h. The hourly forecasts were generated by a ``zero-inflated'' Attention Residual U-Net that outputs the parameters of a probability distribution including a probability of no precipitation and a weighted mixture of two Gamma distributions at each grid point for each hourly forecast lead time. The six-hourly network passes the six consecutive hourly parameter sets, together with summary statistics of the spatial texture of the raw deterministic forecast, through a small recurrent (GRU) layer and a multi-layer perceptron, and maps them to a corresponding zero-inflated mixture of three Gamma distributions describing the six-hourly accumulated precipitation. Training uses sets of hourly probabilistic forecasts, drawn preferentially from wet and heavy-precipitation cases (importance sampling), and matched Multi-Radar Multi-Sensor (MRMS) six-hourly precipitation accumulations, subject to a quality threshold. The resulting six-hourly probabilistic forecasts are well calibrated and skillful, as demonstrated by reliability diagrams, performance diagrams and Brier Skill Scores evaluated over an out-of-sample period spanning day 12 through the end of every month of 2025. The Brier Skill Scores are consistently and significantly higher than those of a baseline that sums independent draws from the hourly distributions. Forecasts show realistic modulation of precipitation related to terrain variations
item.dc:creator: Thomas M Hamill

item.title: Can LLM Agents Improve Imperfect Earth System Model Parameterizations?
item.description: arXiv:2611.03543v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth system models (ESMs) rely on parameterizations to represent unresolved processes such as convection, cloud microphysics, and turbulence. However, translating advances in physical understanding into stable, validated parameterizations and integrating them into ESMs often takes years. Agentic AI could accelerate this process and enable more systematic exploration of design choices. Using warm-rain collision-coalescence as a test case, we evaluate agents' ability to synthesize scientific literature, reimplement published bulk parameterizations, and propose new functional forms as differentiable JAX code. We compare conventional parameterizations, data-driven emulators, and agent-generated closures against high-fidelity superdroplet simulations, repeating unattended experiments across ten language models. With expert guidance or iterative feedback, agents produced executable, differentiable, mass-conserving code, although unattended performance depended strongly on the scheme and language model. Iterative feedback lowered median rollout error for eight of ten models. Retuned physical schemes matched or outperformed many learned parameterizations at substantially lower computational cost, but two of 100 unattended agent-generated closures achieved slightly lower rain-mass error than the most accurate retuned scheme on held-out simulations.
item.dc:creator: Kara D. Lamb

item.title: Sensitivity of the IceCube atmospheric muon rate to decadal trends in the effective atmospheric temperature
item.description: arXiv:2611.00918v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Decadal changes in the Antarctic stratosphere, generally associated with ozone recovery and shifts in polar circulation, are of broad geophysical interest. However, independent long-term measurements of the atmosphere above the Antarctic interior are scarce. We assess whether the atmospheric muon rate recorded by IceCube could constrain decadal changes in the effective atmospheric temperature, $T_\mathrm{eff}$, a weighted average of temperature through the atmosphere that is most sensitive to the stratosphere. Using public atmospheric reanalysis data and records of cosmic-ray, solar, and geomagnetic variability, we reproduce the measured seasonal response of the IceCube muon rate. We then test whether the same response applies to long-term temperature changes with a different vertical temperature profile. The limiting requirement is detector stability rather than counting statistics: an unmodeled muon rate drift of $1\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$ would mimic a temperature trend of $2.8\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. The long-term rate must therefore be stable to approximately $0.3\%\,\mathrm{decade^{-1}}$. Within this budget, snow accumulation contributions can be constrained. For a 14-year record, atmospheric variability gives a one-sided 95% CL statistical sensitivity of $1.6\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$. Given this sensitivity, the $\sim0.9\,\mathrm{K\,decade^{-1}}$ cooling indicated by the 2011-2025 atmospheric records would become distinguishable after approximately 30 years of measurement.
item.dc:creator: Tanvi Krishnan, Gabriela Barenboim, Carlos A. Arg\"uelles

item.title: Sonny-ENS: demystifying machine-learning ensemble weather forecasting
item.description: arXiv:2611.01614v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Every weather forecast is uncertain, and decisions from flood warnings to energy trading depend on how well that uncertainty is quantified. Machine-learning (ML) ensembles now quantify it better than the best physics-based ensemble, yet two things about them remain opaque: whether their skill requires hundreds to thousands of accelerator-days of training, and how a network with a simple source of randomness produces a spread that follows the flow. Here we introduce Sonny-ENS, an ensemble of three 68.9-million-parameter networks with Monte Carlo dropout, trained on the continuous ranked probability score (CRPS) in 2.7 A40 GPU-days. On 2022, it has a lower CRPS than the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts ensemble (ENS) on 96% of 570 targets and an 8.3% lower mean CRPS at lead times of 1-10 days. It outperforms the operational GenCast on 69% of the targets, and a 51-member, 15-day forecast takes 69 s on one GPU. Ablations identify the ingredients of this skill, and a Kolmogorov-Arnold sparse autoencoder shows that dropout injects uncertainty mainly in the tropics, whereas the spread grows where the atmosphere is baroclinically unstable (spatial correlation 0.91 with the Eady growth rate). Skillful probabilistic weather forecasts are therefore within reach of a single GPU server.
item.dc:creator: Minjong Cheon

item.title: Skillful Thunderstorm Forecasts Learned Directly from Observations
item.description: arXiv:2601.17268v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Nowcasting the evolution of severe convective storms over the first few hours after observations are collected is critical for issuing timely, accurate warnings. Forecast accuracy is hindered because the variables that matter most, such as rain, hail, and lightning, are imperfectly represented by numerical model physics and are difficult to initialize correctly. Here we introduce StormScope, a computationally efficient generative forecasting system that learns storm-scale evolution directly from satellite, radar, and lightning observations over the continental United States with no numerical model used for training or initialization. StormScope produces coherent, physically plausible storm trajectories with well-calibrated uncertainty. Across more than 900 forecasts, it greatly exceeds the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's state-of-the-art forthcoming operational numerical modeling system in both deterministic and probabilistic skill through the 0-2-h nowcasting window. StormScope's skill for strong radar echoes exceeds the operational state of the art by approximately 75% and 45% at lead times of 30 min and 2 h, a relative improvement several times larger than machine learning has delivered for global medium-range forecasting. Crucially, it also anticipates storms that develop after forecast initialization, establishing its utility beyond extrapolation of existing radar echoes. It likewise surpasses a leading AI nowcasting model for intense precipitation. Together, these results establish learning directly from observations as a route toward skillful, well-calibrated storm-scale forecasts that is unconstrained by the initialization and microphysics bottlenecks limiting numerical models and their emulators.
item.dc:creator: Jaideep Pathak, Mohammad Shoaib Abbas, Peter Harrington, Corey Potvin, Adam Clark, Patrick Skinner, Aayush Gupta, Tao Ge, Suman Ravuri, Corey Adams, Noah Brenowitz, Alberto Carpentieri, Jason Stock, Jussi Leinonen, Zeyuan Hu, Oliver Hennigh, Nicholas Geneva, Mike Pritchard, Dale Durran

item.title: Watch an AI Weather Model Learn (and Overshoot) Tropical Cyclones
item.description: arXiv:2603.20541v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In a changing climate, artificial intelligence (AI) weather models have the potential to provide cheaper, faster, and more accurate forecasts of high-impact weather events. To realize this potential and gauge trustworthiness, there is a need for more research on how models learn extreme events and how that learning might be improved. Here, we investigate how a Spherical Fourier Neural Operator (SFNO) learns tropical cyclones (TCs) by saving every checkpoint from training and analyzing storm-specific metrics. We find that a subset of storms show early TC intensity forecast skill that degrades into systematic overprediction in the second half of training. Moisture perturbation experiments show a causal relationship between anomalously moist environments and this skill degradation. This work provides a first example of leveraging task-specific training dynamics to further our understanding of how AI weather models learn extreme events.
item.dc:creator: Rebecca Baiman, Ankur Mahesh, Elizabeth A. Barnes

item.title: GraphCast Skill and Systematic Biases in Indian Summer Monsoon Forecasts: Evaluation Against ERA5 and IMERG
item.description: arXiv:2607.11905v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The Indian Summer Monsoon (ISM) is one of the most dynamically complex phenomena in the global climate system, yet its accurate prediction remains challenging for both physics-based and data-driven models. This study presents a systematic climatological evaluation of Google's GraphCast, a machine-learning global weather prediction system, against ERA-5 reanalysis and IMERG satellite precipitation for the boreal summer season (June-September, JJAS) over 2021-2024. We analyze deterministic GraphCast forecasts initialized at 00 UTC across 6-hourly steps to assess +24h, +48h, and +72h performance over the full ISM domain. The evaluation covers the climatological mean state (spatial rainfall, surface temperature, low-level winds), rainfall intensity distributions, thermodynamic drivers (tropospheric temperature gradient, DTT; apparent heat source and moisture sink, Q1 and Q2), monsoon dynamics (vertical wind shear, meridional structure), and variability across intraseasonal, synoptic, and spectral scales. GraphCast reproduces the spatial pattern and annual cycle of monsoon rainfall with high fidelity at short leads, showing a near-zero domain-averaged rainfall bias over the core monsoon zone (-0.7 to -1.2 mm/day) and high daily temporal correlation with IMERG (0.89-0.92). However, temporal variance is moderately suppressed across timescales (power-spectrum variance ratio ~0.63), and the intensity distribution systematically underrepresents extreme events and the 95th percentile. GraphCast closely captures the vertical structure and seasonal evolution of Q1 and Q2, but degrades in northward-propagating intraseasonal variability. Overall, GraphCast shows a moderate underrepresentation of rainfall intensity and variance rather than a wet bias or variance collapse, providing benchmark diagnostics for AI weather models.
item.dc:creator: Somnath Luitel, Parthasarathi Mukhopadhyay, Manmeet Singh, Sandeep Juneja, Saptarishi Dhanuka

item.title: Explainable AI for Geoscientific Regression: Evaluating Sensitivity and Attribution Methods with the Lorenz-63 System and Applications
item.description: arXiv:2608.07406v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) moves from research prototypes to operational tools in Earth system science, trust in its predictions becomes increasingly important. Explainable AI (XAI) offers insight into how AI models make predictions. However, many influential XAI methods were developed or popularised for classification, and their interpretation for regression, which dominates geoscience, is less well established. A central obstacle is the lack of ground truth for judging explanations. We show that, for a dynamical system with known governing equations, matched references can be built directly from the physics. We extend established sensitivity methods to provide physical references for both sensitivity and attribution, separately for methods with implicit and explicit baselines, all computed from the governing equations independently of the network. Applied to an AI emulator of the Lorenz-63 system, these references show that method families answer distinct questions rather than approximating one ``true'' explanation. The emulator's sensitivities and attributions can depart most from their physical references where it forecasts best, so predictive skill is not a substitute for the physical realism of what a model has learned. We then review XAI applications to Earth system regression, organised by method family, extending to issues an idealised system cannot address: computational scalability, strongly correlated high-dimensional predictors, and reliance on expert judgement where no physical reference exists. We also discuss how an XAI method can be mathematically valid yet only partially relevant to a given stakeholder group. We close with future directions and practical recommendations for responsible XAI use in geoscientific modelling and forecasting.
item.dc:creator: Ieuan Higgs, Todd Jones, Kieran Hunt, Anna-Louise Ellis

item.title: An Enhanced Spectral Boundary Integral Method for Modeling Highly Nonlinear Water Waves in Variable Depth
item.description: arXiv:2310.19840v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: This paper presents a new numerical model based on the highly nonlinear potential flow theory for simulating the propagation of water waves in variable depth. A new set of equations for estimating the surface vertical velocity is derived based on the boundary integral equation considering the water depth variability. A successive approximation scheme is also proposed in this study for calculating the surface vertical velocity. With the usage of Fast Fourier Transform, the model can be efficiently used for simulating highly nonlinear water waves on large spatiotemporal scale in a phase-resolving approach. The new model is comprehensively verified and validated through simulating a variety of nonlinear wave phenomenon including free propagating solitary wave, wave transformations over submerged bar, Bragg reflection over undulating bars, nonlinear evolution of Peregrine breather, obliquely propagating uniform waves and extreme waves in crossing random seas. Good agreements are achieved between the numerical simulations and laboratory measurements, indicating that the new model is sufficiently accurate. A discussion is presented on the accuracy and efficiency of the present model, which is compared with the Higher-Order Spectral method. The results show that the present model can be significantly more efficient at the same level of accuracy. It is suggested that the new model developed in the paper can be reliably used to simulate the nonlinear evolution of ocean waves in phase-resolving approach to shed light on the dynamics of nonlinear wave phenomenon taking place on a large spatiotemporal scale, which may be computationally expensive by using other existing methods.
item.dc:creator: Jinghua Wang

item.title: Causal-prior-constrained deep learning for rapid-intensification warning of western North Pacific tropical cyclones
item.description: arXiv:2610.40304v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Rapid intensification (RI) is one of the most dangerous and unpredictable phases of tropical cyclones, and its environmental and structural drivers are difficult to identify and separate in observations. Here we introduce CausalVisionRI, a causal-prior-constrained deep-learning system for 24-h RI warning in the western North Pacific. It integrates infrared remote sensing imagery, atmospheric and oceanic fields, and an observationally discovered causal graph into a unified model. The graph and eight sign-verified effects on 24-h intensity change provide an auditable causal prior for training. Discovered from 522 cyclones in 2000-2017, it identifies causal pathways linking atmospheric and oceanic conditions, the cyclone's dynamical and structural state, and its 24-h intensity change. On a forward holdout covering 2020-2024 and 3,004 records, the five-member ensemble achieves a Brier skill score (BSS) of 0.259 relative to a fixed development climatology, significantly exceeding four reference systems; the three LDA baselines reach at most 0.105. It also attains higher detection rates than a published knowledge-block scheme and a reconstructed contrastive-learning scheme at matched false-detection rates under our USA 30-kt standard and the published RITCF standard. Ablations show that the graph pathway adds 0.032 BSS across the holdout and 0.063 over 2020-2021, with a significant contribution in one ensemble member. A deep-learning model constrained by observationally discovered causal structure thus offers a new route to physically informed RI warning.
item.dc:creator: Xinrui Li, Yijun Jin, Yifan Dong, Shoujuan Shu
